..
Issued at 1028 PM MDT Thu Aug 13 2026

It was a little more active today, at least over the Gila Region
in terms of convection, but fairly quiet everywhere else. Now
we're faced with a very similar scenario to last night. A very
weak outflow boundary is once again drifting across El Paso,
though without sparking off any little renegade showers. Widely
scattered storms are present across Chihuahua just south of
Ahumada, and several CAMS runs show shower and isolated
thunderstorm activity again drifting north into parts of El Paso
and Hudspeth Counties in the wee hours, after about 1-2 AM. The
RRFS members have a little more consistency than usual, and they
favor pulling precip up a little further to the west than recent
HRRR runs, clipping eastern El Paso, and perhaps maintaining
clouds and light showers or sprinkles for a couple hours after
sunrise. Once again played the PoPs very close to ELP, with slight
chance PoPs (20 percent) generally over the west side, and ramping
up to about 40-50 in the far east side of town. Better chances
(60 percent) will be over east El Paso County into far western
Hudspeth.

Water vapor imagery and upper air analysis shows a broad upper
tropospheric low centered over northeastern Mexico, with a closed
low even showing up down to about 500 mb. It fits conceptual
models pretty nicely, with mid-level westerlies kicking off an MCS
in northern Sinaloa, aided by upper level divergence well west of
the low. A tongue of mid-level dry air extends across the Arklatex
region down towards the lower Pecos valley, and another area of
diminishing convection extends from eastern Chihuahua up through
the Trans-Pecos region...in the vicinity of a weak surface trough
and an ill-defined PV anomaly around the 345K level, where you'd
expect it to be in relation to the upper low. 

Meanwhile, mid-level southwesterly flow continues to stream
moisture from the Sierra Madres up into the area. But the uptick
in PWAT values has mostly gone to waste due to a lack of forcing 
and so-so instability (skinny CAPE profiles, and a bit of CIN if 
you consider the mixed layer as a parcel starting point). 

So really, the main driver the next few days will be that upper
tropospheric low. But it will be crawling west overnight, with the
favored area for convection setting up nearly in the same spot in
"near west" Texas tomorrow. Convective debris and stabilization
from any overnight showers and storms should quash precip chances
in and around El Paso tomorrow. Further west, we'll see a near
repeat of today around the Gila and maybe a few storms down in the
Bootheel. 

Saturday is the most favorable day as the upper low drifts into
Coahuila. The PV anomaly band drifts into areas east of the Rio
Grande, just behind a high-level deformation zone. Essentially the
favored area just to our east will finally drift over us. A bit of
low level SE flow will help top-off the low level moisture levels
a bit. Expect widespread, "beefier" convection over the Sacramento
Mountains Saturday afternoon, and a secondary focus over the Black
Range, with NE to SW storm motions favoring outflow convergence in
the lowlands during the evening. Not everyone will see rain,
obviously, but coverage will be greater than the past several
days. 

Sunday, we'll have to deal with convective debris and
stabilizationconcerns, especially east of the Divide. The upper 
low will barely inch into eastern Chihuahua, focusing the better 
upper level support for storms over SW New Mexico. Some drier mid-
level air will work into eastern areas, but the dry tongue will be
slowly filling in a bit. 500 mb temps will climb from around -6C 
Saturday to -4C Sunday over eastern areas too, further supporting 
a dropoff in convection chances east of the Divide for Sunday.

The upper low, or perhaps weakened into an inverted trough, will
pass just to our south Sunday night, usually the least-favored
region for upper support. Sometimes the backside of these things
can bring another uptick, but the inverted trough looks to dampen
out for Monday.

We'll still be in monsoonal easterly flow aloft, but the
subtropical ridge will be sprawling back to the west again, with
some warmer/drier air working in as well. This favors a downtick
in convection chances early next week, with temperatures
attempting to tick back up towards the 100 degree mark in the
lowlands again. Perhaps some relief mid-week as a weak trough
tries to drop down the eastern edge of the ridge? Long way to go.
